text:
After reading about the dangers threatening Russia, about the hopes placed by the sovereign in Moscow, and especially in its renowned nobility, Sonya, with a tremor in her voice arising chiefly from the attention with which she was being listened to, read the final words: “We shall not delay in coming personally into the midst of our people in this capital and in other places of our realm, to confer and to direct all our levies, both those now barring the enemy’s way and those newly raised to strike him down wherever he may appear. May the destruction into which he thinks to cast us recoil upon his own head, and may Europe, freed from bondage, magnify the name of Russia!”

“There, now! That’s the way!” cried the count, opening his moist eyes and pausing several times to snuffle, as though a bottle of strong vinegar salts were being held to his nose. “The sovereign need only say the word, and we shall sacrifice everything and begrudge nothing.”

Shinshin had not yet had time to make the joke he had prepared about the count’s patriotism when Natasha sprang up from her seat and ran over to her father.

“What a darling this papa is!” she said, kissing him, and she looked at Pierre again with that unconscious coquetry which had returned to her together with her animation.

“There’s a patriot for you!” said Shinshin.

“I’m not a patriot at all, but simply...” Natasha replied, offended. “Everything is a joke to you, but this is no joke at all...”

“What jokes!” the count repeated. “He need only say the word, and we shall all go... We’re not some sort of Germans...”

“But did you notice,” said Pierre, “that it says, ‘to confer’?”

“Well, whatever it may be for...”

At that moment Petya, to whom no one was paying any attention, went up to his father and, red all over, said in a breaking voice, now deep, now shrill:

“Well, now, Papa, I shall say it once and for all—and Mama too, as you please—I shall say it once and for all: you must let me enter military service, because I cannot... that is all...”

The countess raised her eyes to heaven in horror, threw up her hands, and turned angrily to her husband.

“There, that’s what your talk has led to!” she said.

But the count recovered from his emotion that very moment.

“Come, come,” he said. “Here’s another warrior! Stop this nonsense: you must study.”

“It is not nonsense, Papa. Fedya Obolensky is younger than I am and he is going too, and most importantly, it makes no difference, I cannot learn anything now, when...” Petya stopped, flushed until he broke into a sweat, and said after all, “when the fatherland is in danger.”

“That will do, that will do—nonsense...”

“But you yourself said that we would sacrifice everything.”

“Petya! I am telling you to be quiet,” shouted the count, glancing at his wife, who had gone pale and was staring fixedly at her younger son.

“And I am telling you. Pyotr Kirillovich will say so too...”

“I am telling you—it is rubbish; the milk is not yet dry on your lips, and you want to enter military service! Come, come, I am telling you,” and the count, taking the papers with him, probably to read them once more in his study before resting, left the room.

“Pyotr Kirillovich, well then, let us go and have a smoke...”

Pierre was in a state of confusion and indecision. Natasha’s unaccustomedly shining and animated eyes, constantly turning toward him with more than tenderness, had brought him into this state.

“No, I think I shall go home...”

“Home? But you meant to spend the evening with us... And you have begun coming so rarely as it is. And this girl of mine...” said the count good-naturedly, pointing to Natasha, “is cheerful only when you are here...”

“Yes, I had forgotten... I absolutely must go home... Business...” Pierre said hurriedly.

“Well then, good-bye,” said the count, finally leaving the room.

“Why are you leaving? Why are you upset? Why?...” Natasha asked Pierre, looking challengingly into his eyes.

“Because I love you!” he wanted to say, but he did not say it; he flushed to the point of tears and lowered his eyes.

“Because it is better for me to visit you less often... Because... no, I simply have business...”

“Why? No, tell me,” Natasha began resolutely, and suddenly fell silent. They both looked at each other in fear and confusion. He tried to smile, but could not: his smile expressed suffering, and he silently kissed her hand and went out.

Pierre resolved within himself not to visit the Rostovs anymore.

XXI.

After receiving this categorical refusal, Petya went to his room and there, having locked himself away from everyone, wept bitterly. Everyone behaved as though they had noticed nothing when he came to tea, silent and gloomy, with tear-stained eyes.

The next day the sovereign arrived. Several of the Rostovs’ household servants asked leave to go and see the Tsar. That morning Petya spent a long time dressing, combing his hair, and arranging his collars the way grown men did. He frowned at himself in the mirror, made gestures, shrugged his shoulders, and finally, without telling anyone, put on his forage cap and left the house by the back steps, trying not to be noticed. Petya had resolved to go straight to the place where the sovereign was and to explain directly to some chamberlain (Petya imagined that the sovereign was always surrounded by chamberlains) that he, Count Rostov, despite his youth, wished to serve the fatherland, that youth could be no obstacle to devotion, and that he was ready... While getting dressed, Petya had prepared many splendid words that he would say to the chamberlain.

Petya counted on the success of his presentation to the sovereign precisely because he was a child (Petya even thought how everyone would marvel at his youth), while at the same time, in the arrangement of his collars, in his hairstyle, and in his sedate, deliberate gait, he wanted to present himself as an old man. But the farther he walked, and the more he was distracted by the ever-growing crowds arriving at the Kremlin, the more he forgot to maintain the sedateness and deliberateness proper to grown men. As he approached the Kremlin, he began to concern himself with not being jostled and resolutely thrust out his elbows on either side with a menacing air. But at the Trinity Gate, despite all his resolution, people who probably did not know the patriotic purpose for which he was going to the Kremlin pressed him so hard against the wall that he had to submit and stop while carriages passed through the gate with a rumbling sound echoing beneath the arches. Beside Petya stood a peasant woman with a footman, two merchants, and a retired soldier. After standing in the gate for some time, Petya, without waiting for all the carriages to pass, wanted to move on before the others and began resolutely working with his elbows; but the woman standing opposite him, at whom he first directed his elbows, shouted at him angrily:

“Why are you pushing, young master? You can see everyone is standing still. Why must you shove your way through?”

“Then everyone will start shoving through,” said the footman, and, also beginning to work with his elbows, he squeezed Petya into a stinking corner of the gateway.

Petya wiped away with his hands the sweat covering his face and straightened his collars, which had gone limp with sweat and which he had arranged so well at home, the way grown men did.

Petya felt that he looked unpresentable and was afraid that if he appeared before the chamberlains in such a state, he would not be admitted to the sovereign. But there was no possibility of tidying himself up or moving to another place because of the crush. One of the generals passing by was an acquaintance of the Rostovs. Petya wanted to ask for his help, but considered that this would be contrary to courage. When all the carriages had passed, the crowd surged forward and swept Petya out into the square, which was completely filled with people. There were people not only in the square, but on the slopes, on the roofs—everywhere. No sooner had Petya found himself in the square than he distinctly heard the sounds of bells and the joyful murmur of the people filling the entire Kremlin.
